title: vector-sdk-py: discord.py-style Vector Bots
subtitle: Write Vector messenger bots in Python with the discord.py API, on top of the Rust vector_sdk, with Python labs
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A hands-on course based on lucky-edgelord/vector-sdk-py (MIT, alpha), a discord.py-style Python library for Vector messenger bots built on the official Rust vector_sdk with PyO3. Learn the mapping from discord.py, installing and keys, events (including Vector's own), prefix and native slash commands with type hints, cogs, checks, cooldowns and tasks, embeds rendered as markdown, views built from reactions, community moderation, voice, Mini Apps and the development workflow. Labs run offline and simulate the library's rules in Python.

chapters.title: What vector-sdk-py is and how it maps from discord.py
summary: vector-sdk-py is a Python library for Vector messenger bots. It copies the discord.py style: the same decorators, cogs, ctx, checks, cooldowns, converters, wait_for, tasks.loop, embeds and views.

Underneath, every network, crypto and storage call runs in the official Rust vector_sdk crate, compiled into the package with PyO3. You get its communities, private messages, Mini Apps and voice without writing Rust.
The repository is github.com/lucky-edgelord/vector-sdk-py, MIT licensed, marked alpha, and needs Python 3.9 or newer. Most discord.py bots port by changing the imports.

glossary.def: A Rust library for writing Python extension modules.
One compiled package that works across Python versions on a platform.
Vector's name for a Discord guild; Guild is kept as an alias.
A Vector user's public key, used as the user id.
The raw Rust bot, reachable as bot.native for anything not wrapped.

keyPoints: import vector; from vector.ext import commands, tasks.
Layers: src/ is the PyO3 binding, python/vector/ is the discord.py style API.
Guild is an alias of Community; user.id is an alias of npub.
Intents are accepted and ignored: Vector sends every event.
Anything not wrapped is reachable through bot.native.

items: ELI5. It is a translator in a costume. It dresses a secret-letter robot from the Rust world to look and act just like the Discord robot you already know.

If you can write a discord.py bot, you already know this library. The idea is to keep your habits and swap the engine. The Python layer looks like discord.py, and the Rust layer does the secure messaging.

lesson.code:
import os
import vector
from vector.ext import commands

bot = commands.Bot(command_prefix="!")

@bot.event
async def on_ready():
    print(f"Logged in as {bot.user}")

@bot.command()
async def ping(ctx):
    await ctx.reply("pong")

bot.run(os.environ.get("VECTOR_NSEC"))

items: Both the prefix command and Vector's native slash command work for ping. Every command is also published to the bot's manifest, so it appears in Vector's slash picker with typed arguments.

Porting is mostly renaming. Import vector as discord, or just use vector. Guild becomes Community with Guild kept as an alias, user.id becomes user.npub with id kept as an alias, and Intents are accepted but ignored because Vector delivers every event.

Some things have no direct equivalent and are emulated. Vector has no message components, so views are built from reactions. Embeds are rendered as coloured markdown. Ephemeral replies are sent as direct messages. The next chapters explain each emulation.
Because the project is alpha, expect change. Read the README and the tests for the current behaviour, and remember the Rust crate underneath also changes quickly.

practice.title: Same user?
practice.intro: Write same_user(a, b): users are dictionaries; return True when they have the same 'npub', or when one has 'npub' and the other has 'id' with the same value (id is an alias).
practice.solution:
def same_user(a, b):
    ka = a.get('npub', a.get('id'))
    kb = b.get('npub', b.get('id'))
    return ka is not None and ka == kb

practice.title: Python supported?
practice.intro: Write py_ok(version): True when a version string like '3.9.1' is 3.9 or newer (major 3).
practice.solution:
def py_ok(version):
    p = version.split('.')
    major = int(p[0])
    minor = int(p[1])
    if major != 3:
        return major > 3
    return minor >= 9

chapters.title: Installing, keys and starting the bot

maps.title: Setup
links: pip install git+... | builds | Rust SDK
Rust and cmake | are needed for | Build

summary: Install with pip install git+https://github.com/lucky-edgelord/vector-sdk-py. This compiles the Rust SDK, so you need a Rust toolchain and cmake for the Opus voice codec. Prebuilt wheels are produced by the GitHub Actions workflow, and once published to PyPI it will be pip install vector-sdk-py.

A Vector identity is a Nostr key. bot.run takes an nsec key where discord.py takes a token. Called with no key it reuses the key stored in data_dir, which defaults to ./vector-bot-data, creating one on first run. A seed phrase works with mnemonic.
Voice and Mini Apps are built by default. Speech to text (whisper), Tor and I2P are opt-in build features, and Client.features() tells you what your build has.

glossary.def: The bot's private key; plays the role of a Discord token.
Where the bot keeps its database and key; default ./vector-bot-data.
manual (default), public, or a whitelist of npubs.
The build tool that compiles the Rust extension into a Python package.
A prebuilt Python package file.

keyPoints: Needs Rust toolchain and cmake to build from source.
bot.run(nsec) or bot.run() to reuse the stored key.
vector.generate_nsec() mints a key; keep it secret.
invite_policy: manual, public, or whitelist=[npubs].
Whisper, Tor and I2P are opt-in features at build time.

items: ELI5. To start, you need a toolbox to build the robot, and a secret code. If you give no code, the robot makes one and keeps it in its own drawer.

Installing this library is different from most Python packages because it compiles Rust. That takes a few minutes the first time, and later installs reuse the cache. Prebuilt wheels avoid the compile when they are available for your platform.

lesson.code:
pip install git+https://github.com/lucky-edgelord/vector-sdk-py

# opt-in features at build time
pip install "git+https://github.com/lucky-edgelord/vector-sdk-py" \
    --config-settings=build-args="--features whisper,tor"

items: Your bot's identity is a Nostr key. Where discord.py wants a token, this library wants the nsec. If you pass nothing, the library reuses the key it saved in data_dir, and creates one on the first run, which is perfect for experiments.

lesson.code:
import vector
print(vector.generate_nsec())   # mint one and keep it secret

bot = commands.Bot(command_prefix="!",
                   data_dir="./vector-bot-data",
                   invite_policy="public")        # or "manual" or whitelist=[...]
bot.run(os.environ.get("VECTOR_NSEC"))

items: Invite policy decides what happens when someone invites the bot to a community. Manual queues the invite and fires on_community_invite, where you can call invite.accept. Public accepts every invite. A whitelist accepts only invites from the npubs you list.
Treat the nsec like a password: read it from an environment variable, never commit it, and do not print it. Give each bot its own data_dir, because the directory holds the key and the database.

chapters.title: Events: the discord.py names plus Vector's own
summary: The usual discord.py event names fire with the usual arguments: on_ready, on_message, on_message_edit, on_message_delete, on_reaction_add, on_typing, on_member_join, on_member_remove, on_member_ban, on_guild_join, on_guild_role_create and more.

Vector adds events of its own: on_community_invite, on_community_change, on_member_kick, on_member_timeout, on_member_roles_update, on_overwrite_update, on_channel_keyed, on_community_dissolve, on_xdc_presence, on_xdc_session and on_slash_command.
Register with bot.event or bot.listen, and use wait_for when you want to pause a command until a particular event arrives.

glossary.def: An extra handler for an event, added with bot.listen so several can coexist.
The raw form of every audited community change; other events derive from it.
A kick; Discord folds this into on_member_remove.
The bot received the key for a private channel.
Await one event that passes a check, with a timeout.

keyPoints: bot.event replaces a handler; bot.listen adds one.
Vector extras: on_community_invite, on_member_kick, on_member_timeout.
on_member_roles_update(member, added, removed) is finer than on_member_update.
on_slash_command(name, args, message) sees raw native commands.
Use wait_for with a check and a timeout.

items: ELI5. Events are doorbells. Some are the same as in Discord, and some are new bells for things only this club has, like time-outs.
Events work the way they do in discord.py. A decorated coroutine with the right name is called when the event happens. The names and arguments match closely, so most of your handlers need no change.

Vector's richer community model produces events that Discord does not have. A timeout, a role change, a nickname change and a permission overwrite each get their own event, and they all derive from on_community_change, which carries the raw change and who made it.

A kick is its own event, on_member_kick, rather than being folded into on_member_remove as Discord does. If you want one handler for both, listen to both. The on_member_ban and on_member_unban events behave as in discord.py.

lesson.code:
# wait for the same user's next message, up to 30 seconds
def check(m):
    return m.author == ctx.author and m.channel == ctx.channel

msg = await bot.wait_for("message", check=check, timeout=30)

items: Error handling is the same too. on_error catches exceptions in event handlers, and on_command_error catches errors from commands. Keep handlers short and push long work into tasks, so they do not block other events.

practice.intro: Write roles_diff(before, after): both are lists of role names. Return [added, removed] as sorted lists.

def roles_diff(before, after):
    added = [r for r in after if r not in before]
    removed = [r for r in before if r not in after]
    added.sort()
    removed.sort()
    return [added, removed]

chapters.title: Commands: prefix and native slash at once

maps.title: Commands
links: Type hint | maps to | Vector arg type
More than 8 args | stays | Prefix only

summary: Every command you define is available as a text command and, where possible, as a native Vector slash command. The library publishes a manifest so the command appears in Vector's slash picker with typed arguments, and Vector checks the types before your code runs.

Type hints decide the argument types: str is text, int is int, float is number, bool is a flag, Member or User is a user picker, Literal is a choice. Trailing arguments such as a keyword-only rest, args or Greedy become trailing text. Anything else is text, converted in Python.
The default prefix is the slash. Set a prefix such as an exclamation mark to also accept text commands. Commands whose name or signature cannot be expressed natively stay prefix only.

glossary.def: The list of native commands published to Vector.
A typing construct that limits a value to fixed options; shown as a dropdown.
A converter wrapper that consumes as many arguments as possible.
A decorator that gives each argument a description in the picker.
A command usable as both text and native slash; here every command is.

keyPoints: command_prefix defaults to '/' (native only); '!' also accepts text.
str=text, int=int, float=number, bool=flag, Member=user, Literal=choice.
Rest, *args and Greedy become trailing text.
Names with uppercase letters or more than 8 args stay prefix only.
Groups become /name subcommand args.

items: ELI5. A command is a magic word that works two ways: type it, or pick it from a menu that has the blanks already drawn for you.

The nice thing is that you write one function and get two ways to call it. A person can type an exclamation mark and the command name, or pick the slash command from the picker and fill in typed fields.

This is published as convert with a number field called temp and a choice called unit with the options c and f. Vector checks the input and replies with usage before your function runs, so you rarely need to validate.

Not everything can be native. Arguments that are a Role, a TextChannel or a custom converter are sent as text and converted in Python. A command whose name has uppercase letters, or which has more than eight arguments, stays prefix only, and a log line tells you so.

Groups work like in discord.py: bot.group makes a command with subcommands, published as a name followed by a subcommand and its arguments. Load your cogs in setup_hook, as discord.py recommends, so their commands are part of the manifest published at startup.

Prefix commands still use the familiar error classes. A bad conversion raises BadArgument, a missing value raises MissingRequiredArgument, and an unknown command raises CommandNotFound, which you can handle in on_command_error.

chapters.title: Cogs, checks, cooldowns, converters and tasks
summary: Structure works as in discord.py. A Cog groups commands and listeners, and an extension module defines async def setup(bot) that adds it with bot.add_cog. Cog_check can apply a rule to every command in a cog.

Checks such as has_permissions, guild_only and is_owner guard commands. Cooldowns limit how often a command can be used, per user, community, channel or other bucket. is_owner uses owner_id, which takes an npub.

Converters turn text into objects: Member, Role, TextChannel, Greedy, Range, Literal and your own. tasks.loop repeats a coroutine on a schedule. Errors are classes such as MissingPermissions, BadArgument and CommandOnCooldown.

glossary.def: A class grouping related commands and listeners.
A predicate a command must pass, such as has_permissions or guild_only.
A limit of rate uses per period seconds in a bucket.
The scope of a cooldown: default, user, guild/community, channel, member, category or role.
A decorator that runs a coroutine every seconds, minutes or hours.

keyPoints: await bot.add_cog(Cog(bot)) inside async def setup(bot).
cog_check can guard every command in a cog.
@commands.cooldown(rate, per, BucketType.user).
has_permissions(kick_members=True), is_owner(), guild_only().
@tasks.loop(minutes=5); start with .start().

items: ELI5. A cog is a toy box, a check is a bouncer, and a cooldown is a rule that says you only get a few turns every little while.

Cogs keep a growing bot tidy. Each cog is a class with its own commands and listeners, and the bot loads them from extension modules. The examples directory has a cogs bot with moderation, fun and admin cogs.

Checks run before the command body. If one fails, a CheckFailure subclass such as MissingPermissions is raised and goes to your error handler, so you can answer politely. A cog level error handler can be attached with the command's error decorator.

A cooldown is a token bucket. A command allows rate uses within each period of per seconds. Once the tokens are used up, the next call raises CommandOnCooldown carrying how many seconds remain. The bucket type decides who shares the allowance.

Converters work as in discord.py, including Greedy for many arguments and Range for bounds. Errors such as MemberNotFound and RoleNotFound carry the offending argument, which makes friendly error messages easy.

chapters.title: Messages and embeds on a messenger without embeds

maps.title: Messages
links: Inline fields | sit | Side by side

summary: Vector has no embed objects, so vector.Embed keeps discord.py's full API but renders itself into Vector's markdown.
The colour paints the title and a bar character down the left edge, inline fields sit side by side separated by a vertical line, and the timestamp is shown in each reader's own timezone.

Sending works as you expect: send, reply, edit, history, purge, fetch_message, attachments with await attachment.read(), custom emoji reactions and typing indicators. delete_after sets a NIP-40 expiry that every client honours and also deletes the message after that many seconds.
Other emulations are worth knowing: ephemeral replies are sent as a direct message, and deleting someone else's message hides it as a moderation action, while your own messages are really deleted.

glossary.def: A rich card; here rendered as coloured markdown.
The Nostr rule for event expiration; used for delete_after and expires_in.
A reply only the requester should see; sent as a DM in this library.
vector.File wraps a path or bytes to attach to a message.
An image URL on its own line so Vector shows a preview.

keyPoints: Embed API is discord.py's: add_field, set_author, set_footer, set_image, to_dict.
Rendering: bar char, bold title in colour, inline fields joined with a bar.
attachment://name plus file=vector.File(...) sends a real attachment.
delete_after sets expiry and deletes; expires_in sets expiry only.
ephemeral=True sends the reply to the user's DMs.

items: ELI5. This messenger has no fancy cards, so the robot draws one using coloured text. It can also make a message disappear on a timer that every phone obeys.

An embed is just a pretty way to lay out information. Since Vector has no embed object, the library turns it into markdown that looks like one. You write the same code you would for discord.py and the library does the translation.

lesson.code:
embed = vector.Embed(title="Server stats", description="Updated hourly", colour=0x59FCB3)
embed.add_field(name="CPU", value="12%", inline=True)
embed.add_field(name="RAM", value="3.1 GB", inline=True)
embed.set_footer(text="vector-sdk-py")
embed.timestamp = vector.utils.utcnow()
await ctx.send(embed=embed)

items: The rendering puts a coloured bar at the left of every line, then the title in bold, then the description. Two inline fields are drawn on one line separated by a vertical bar. The timestamp uses a time tag, so each reader sees their own timezone.

To send an image as a real attachment, set the embed image to attachment colon slash slash and the file name, and pass the file with the message. The image goes first and the embed becomes its caption. A plain URL image is placed on its own line so Vector shows a link preview.

delete_after is stronger than its Discord cousin. It sets an expiry that every Vector client honours, so the message vanishes even if the bot is offline, and it also schedules a deletion. If you only want the expiry, use expires_in.
Because ephemeral replies become direct messages, think twice before using them in busy chats. And remember that deleting another person's message hides it as moderation rather than erasing it.

practice.title: Render an embed
practice.intro: Write render(title, description, fields): return a list of lines. First '▍ **' + title + '**', then '▍ ' + description, then for each field [name, value] two lines '▍ **' + name + '**' and '▍ ' + value.
practice.solution:
def render(title, description, fields):
    bar = '\u258d'
    out = [bar + ' **' + title + '**', bar + ' ' + description]
    for name, value in fields:
        out.append(bar + ' **' + name + '**')
        out.append(bar + ' ' + value)
    return out

def inline_row(fields):
    sep = ' \u2502 '
    names = sep.join(['**' + n + '**' for n, v in fields])
    values = sep.join([v for n, v in fields])
    return [names, values]

chapters.title: Views, buttons, selects and modals built from reactions
summary: Vector has no message components, so vector.ui builds them from reactions. Each button or select option becomes an emoji reaction that the bot adds under the message, with a legend in the message text. Reacting clicks it, and removing your reaction clicks it again.

Buttons without an emoji get regional letters A, B, C and so on. Select options get number emoji one to ten, then letters. A Modal asks its TextInput fields as a short chat conversation and then calls on_submit. ui.Paginator pages text or embeds with first, previous, next, last and stop reactions.
timeout, on_timeout, interaction_check, stop, wait and interaction.response.edit_message all work as in discord.py.

glossary.def: An emoji reaction added by the bot that acts as a button.
The text in the message that explains which emoji does what.
The object passed to a callback when someone clicks.
A view that pages through a list of pages with arrow reactions.
A form emulated as a conversation of questions.

keyPoints: Same decorators as discord.py: @ui.button, @ui.select, ui.View, ui.Modal.
Buttons: given emoji, else A B C. Options: 1 to 10, then letters.
Reacting clicks; removing the reaction clicks again.
ephemeral=True is sent as a DM.
Reaction limits mean views should stay small.

items: ELI5. There are no buttons here, so the robot sticks little emoji stickers under a message. Tap a sticker and it counts as a button press.

The trick is that reactions are the one interactive thing every message already has. The library adds one reaction per control and listens for people reacting. It feels like buttons even though the mechanism is different.

The message text gets a legend such as a checkmark for confirm, so people know what each reaction does. When someone reacts, your callback runs with an interaction. Calling stop ends the view, and the bot removes its reactions.

Select menus use numbered reactions: an option without its own emoji gets the number for its position, from one to ten, and after ten the regional letters. Because reactions are limited, keep menus short, or use the Paginator.
A Modal is a conversation. The bot asks each TextInput as a short question, waits for the answer, then calls on_submit with all the values. It is slower than a popup but works anywhere a chat does.
Gate who may click with interaction_check, exactly as in discord.py. Without it, anyone who can react can click, so a confirm button in a public channel should check the user.

chapters.title: Communities and moderation
summary: Communities are richer than Discord guilds. You can create communities, join by invite link, preview an invite with fetch_invite, create invites with a lifetime and label, and manage roles, categories, text, voice and forum channels.

Permissions work per channel with set_permissions and overwrites, and permissions_for tells you what someone may do. Moderation includes kick, ban, unban, bulk_ban for one key rotation, member.timeout, nicknames, pins, audit_logs and bans listings, and contain_raid.

Recovery and operations tools include relay management with check_relays and move_relays, refound and repair_roster. leave removes the bot, and delete dissolves the community, which is irreversible and for the owner only.

glossary.def: A shared space with members, roles and channels.
A per-channel permission change for a role or member.
A temporary silence applied to a member.
The list of recorded moderation and settings actions.
Banning many members with a single key rotation.

keyPoints: create_community, join(invite_url), fetch_invite for a preview.
create_role, create_text_channel, create_category, create_forum.
channel.set_permissions(target, send_messages=False) locks a channel.
member.timeout(timedelta), guild.bulk_ban(members), guild.audit_logs().
guild.delete() dissolves a community; owner only, irreversible.

items: ELI5. Running a club means locking rooms, putting people in time-out and banning troublemakers. Dissolving the whole club is the big red button only the owner may press.

Think of running a community as a set of small decisions: who may enter, what they can see, who may speak, and who can undo mistakes. The library exposes each one as a method on the objects you already know from discord.py.

The lock command in the moderation example denies the send permission to the default role in the current channel. The timeout command silences a member for a number of minutes. Both are guarded by permission checks.
When a wave of spam arrives, ban one account at a time and each ban rotates the community key. bulk_ban bans the whole list with a single rekey. contain_raid treats a raid as one moderation unit.

The audit log is an async iterator of entries with a user, an action and a time, which makes a handy command for admins. Because each moderation call is checked the way every member's client will judge it, a refused action raises an error that you should handle.

Dissolving a community with delete cannot be undone and only the owner may do it. Never wire it to a casual command. Require an explicit confirmation from a person, for example with a confirm view that only the owner may click.

chapters.title: Voice, Mini Apps, testing and contributing
summary: Voice works like discord.py. voice_channel.connect returns a client, vc.play plays an FFmpegPCMAudio source, and bots can also listen. Audio is 48 kHz mono 16-bit PCM bytes. utterances yields one clip per speaker per pause, and a Transcriber turns a clip into text in a whisper build.

Mini Apps are WebXDC apps shared in a chat. Decorate an async function with bot.xdc_app(app_id) and iterate the session for data, peer_join and peer_leave events. Sessions end after idle or quiet timeouts.

For development, install maturin and pytest, run maturin develop to build the Rust extension into your virtual environment, and run pytest. The Python layer is tested against a fake native bot, so most tests need no network.

glossary.def: Raw audio samples; here 48 kHz mono 16-bit.
One speaker's clip, cut at a pause.
The bot's live link to one open Mini App.
Builds PyO3 projects into Python packages.
A test double that stands in for the Rust bot.

keyPoints: PCM bytes: 48000 samples per second, mono, 2 bytes per sample.
vc.play(FFmpegPCMAudio(path)); vc.say(pcm); vc.hush().
@bot.xdc_app('id') async def f(session): async for event in session.
event.type: data, peer_join, peer_leave; event.verified_sender names the sender.
maturin develop --release; pytest tests.

items: ELI5. The robot can join voice calls and little shared apps. To help build it, you test with a pretend robot so you do not need the real internet.

Voice turns the bot into a participant in a call. You connect to a voice channel, play audio, and listen. Everything is raw PCM, which keeps the interface simple: bytes in, bytes out. FFmpeg decodes files for you.

lesson.code:
vc = await voice_channel.connect()
vc.play(vector.FFmpegPCMAudio("song.mp3"), after=lambda e: print("done"))

async for member, pcm in vc.utterances():     # bots can listen
    print(member, await transcriber.transcribe(pcm))

items: At 48 kilohertz mono with two bytes per sample, one second of audio is 96 thousand bytes. A twenty millisecond frame is 960 samples, which is 1920 bytes. Knowing these numbers helps when you buffer or cut clips.

A Mini App is a small web app shared in a chat that everyone who opens it uses together. Your bot can be a referee, an opponent or the server behind it. Use verified_sender when you must trust who sent a message, and remember players can see each other's network addresses.

The repository is built for contributors. src is the PyO3 binding, python/vector is the API, and the tests use a fake native bot. A GitHub Actions workflow builds wheels for Linux, macOS and Windows. Add a test whenever you add a feature.
